en: Extremely miserable or hopeless; completely without pride or dignity
hook: AB-JECT: thrown (ject) away (ab), cast down to the lowest point.
story: Abject. After the cyclone, Nasima's family lost their house, their boat, and their two cows in a single night. For weeks they slept under a plastic sheet beside the embankment, with no money and nothing to eat but relief rice. They lived in abject poverty: extremely miserable and hopeless. Abject can also describe behaviour completely without pride, as in an abject apology. Think: ab means away, and ject means thrown, so abject means cast down. Synonyms: wretched, hopeless, servile.

gre.s: Far from the defiant statement his supporters expected, the senator issued an ____ apology, begging forgiveness and conceding every one of his critics' points.
gre.clue: begging forgiveness and conceding every one of his critics' points

example: Caught copying his lab report, Rafi sent the professor an abject email that apologized four times in three short paragraphs.

en: Distant and unfriendly; emotionally reserved
hook: ALOOF: sits ALOFT on the ROOF, far above everyone.
story: Aloof. At the office Eid party, everyone laughed, danced, and swapped plates of biryani. The new manager stood alone by the window with a cup of coffee. He nodded politely when spoken to but never joined a conversation, never smiled, never asked a single question. People assumed he was arrogant. Months later they learned he was simply shy. Still, his manner was aloof: distant, detached, emotionally reserved. Picture someone sitting aloft on a roof, far above everyone else.

gre.s: Although the actress appeared ____ in interviews, rarely smiling or revealing anything personal, her friends describe her as warm and playful.
gre.clue: rarely smiling or revealing anything personal

example: The new striker stayed aloof from his teammates during training, eating lunch alone and skipping the squad's evening card games.

en: Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something
hook: AMBI = both (ambidextrous). Feeling BOTH ways at once.
story: Ambivalent. The email said Congratulations. Rafi had won admission to a university in Canada. He ran to tell his mother, grinning. Then he saw her face, proud and sad at the same time, and his own throat tightened. A new life, but thousands of kilometres from everyone he loved. He felt happy and heartbroken at once. That is ambivalent: having strong, mixed feelings pulling in opposite directions. Ambi means both. It does not mean indifferent; ambivalent people feel a great deal.

gre.s: The critic remained ____ about the novel, admiring its lyrical prose while deploring its sluggish, aimless plot.
gre.clue: admiring its lyrical prose while deploring

example: Nusrat felt ambivalent about the job offer in Chittagong, eager for the higher salary but reluctant to leave her parents in Dhaka.

en: Friendly and without serious disagreement
hook: AMICABLE: AMIGO (friend) + able.
story: Amicable. After ten years as business partners, Farzana and Tamim decided to go their separate ways. There was no shouting, no lawyers, no lawsuits. They divided the clients fairly, shook hands, and still meet for tea every month. Their separation was amicable: friendly and without serious disagreement. Amicable comes from Latin amicus, friend, like amigo in Spanish. Amiable describes a pleasant person; amicable describes relations and agreements. Synonyms: cordial, harmonious, peaceable. Opposite: hostile.

gre.s: Although the negotiations had been tense, the two companies reached an ____ settlement, parting on such good terms that they later launched a joint venture.
gre.clue: parting on such good terms that they later launched a joint venture

example: The two neighbors ended their long quarrel over the shared wall with an amicable chat over tea on the rooftop.

en: Obscure and puzzling, familiar only to a small group of specialists
hook: ARCANE: hidden in an ARK, like secret knowledge only priests can read.
story: Arcane. Every Eid, Rafi's grandfather pulls out a worn deck of cards and tries to teach the grandchildren an old village game. It has thirty-two rules, secret signals, and scoring that changes depending on the moon. Nobody under seventy remembers how it works. By the second round, the children always give up. Those rules are arcane: mysterious and understood by only a few people. Arcane knowledge is hidden, like secrets locked in an ark. Tax law often feels arcane.

gre.s: The scholar's knowledge of ____ medieval manuscripts, which perhaps a dozen people in the world could read, made her indispensable to the museum.
gre.clue: which perhaps a dozen people in the world could read

example: The tax code is so arcane that even experienced accountants in Motijheel sometimes phone colleagues to interpret a single clause.

en: Very strict or serious; extremely plain, without comfort or decoration
hook: AUSTERE sounds like 'a stair' of bare concrete: no carpet, no decoration, just hard steps.
story: Austere. When Rafi visited his grandfather's room for the first time, he looked for the TV. There was none. One wooden chair. One lamp. A shelf with three books. Rice and lentils, every single day, and not a single picture on the walls. "Don't you get bored, Dada?" Rafi asked. The old man smiled. "Less to own, less to worry about." Austere means severely plain and strict, with every comfort stripped away. An austere life, an austere building, an austere teacher.

gre.s: In contrast to the lavish palaces of his predecessors, the new ruler's residence was strikingly ____, furnished with little more than a desk and a cot.
gre.clue: In contrast to the lavish palaces

example: The physics department occupied an austere concrete building with bare walls, metal chairs, and a single flickering lamp in each corridor.

en: Able to stay afloat; lighthearted and hopeful about the future
hook: BUOYANT: like a BUOY, always floating up.
story: Buoyant. On a trip to the Sundarbans, Anika was nervous about the boat ride. The guide handed her a bright orange life jacket and explained that it was buoyant: able to float, and able to keep her floating too. Then she noticed the guide himself. After twenty years on the river, he was still singing and joking, buoyant in spirit: cheerful and optimistic. Both senses mean staying up. A buoy is a floating marker in a harbour. Synonyms: floating, cheerful, upbeat.

gre.s: Investors remained ____ despite the gloomy forecasts, convinced that the economy would rebound within a few months and reward those who held their nerve.
gre.clue: convinced that the economy would rebound within a few months

example: Despite losing the first two matches, the team's mood stayed buoyant, and the players joked loudly on the bus back to Sylhet.

en: Able to burn or corrode chemically; sarcastically bitter and hurtful
hook: CAUSTIC soda burns your skin; caustic words burn your feelings.
story: Caustic. In chemistry lab, the teacher held up a bottle of caustic soda. "Careful. This burns skin." That afternoon, Farhan's group submitted their project and received a different kind of burn. The examiner had written one comment in red: "Did anyone actually try?" The whole group felt it sting. Caustic describes chemicals that corrode and words that wound with bitter sarcasm. A caustic critic burns through your confidence like acid through cloth.

gre.s: The reviewer's ____ wit, which spared neither the actors nor the director, made her columns as feared as they were entertaining.
gre.clue: spared neither the actors nor the director

example: The chemistry teacher warned the class that the caustic solution could burn skin within seconds and insisted everyone wear gloves.

en: A puzzling problem that has no easy answer
hook: CONUNDRUM: a DRUM of confusion banging in your head.
story: Conundrum. Nadia received two offers on the same day: a full scholarship to study economics abroad, and a job at a top bank in Dhaka that would let her support her ailing parents. Accepting one meant losing the other forever. She lay awake for nights, turning it over. It was a real conundrum: a confusing and difficult problem with no easy answer. Originally, a conundrum was a riddle whose answer involved a pun. Synonyms: dilemma, puzzle, quandary, enigma.

gre.s: The dwindling water supply poses a genuine ____ for officials: restricting use would anger farmers, yet doing nothing would leave the city dry within a decade.
gre.clue: restricting use would anger farmers, yet doing nothing would leave the city dry

example: Choosing a university became a real conundrum for Tanvir, since the best program was abroad but his family could not afford the fees.

en: To reduce or cut short
hook: CUR-TAIL: cut the TAIL short.
story: Curtail. The school's annual sports day began brightly. Then the radio announced an approaching cyclone. The principal stopped the races after only two events and sent everyone home. The day had been curtailed: cut short. That year, the government also curtailed its spending, reducing budgets for new buildings. To curtail is to reduce or cut short. Curfews curtail freedom of movement. Think: cutting the tail short.

gre.s: Fearing a budget shortfall, the university was forced to ____ its research programs, eliminating nearly a third of them.
gre.clue: eliminating nearly a third of them

example: Repeated power cuts curtailed evening study hours at the dormitory, so students began gathering under the streetlights to finish their homework.

en: To reduce the value or quality of something
hook: DE-TRACT: TRACT (pull) value AWAY.
story: Detract. Arif's new phone had a beautiful screen, a fast processor, and a superb camera. But the battery died by lunchtime every single day. "It is a great phone," he told his friends, "but the battery really detracts from it." To detract is to reduce the value or quality of something, usually followed by from. De means away and tract means pull, as in tractor: pulling value away. Do not confuse it with distract, to draw attention away. Synonyms: diminish, lessen, take away.

gre.s: A few minor typographical errors do little to ____ from what is otherwise a meticulously researched and elegantly written history.
gre.clue: otherwise a meticulously researched and elegantly written history

example: The noisy air conditioner detracted from an otherwise moving concert, drowning out the softest passages of the sitar solo.

en: Deep hostility; the state of being enemies
hook: ENMITY: ENEMY-ity.
story: Enmity. Two rival shopkeepers in Old Dhaka have not spoken for twenty years. They were once partners, until one accused the other of stealing. Now they cut prices just to hurt each other, warn customers against each other, and even their sons fight in the street. Between them lies deep enmity: hostility, the state of being enemies. Enmity and enemy share a root. Its opposite is amity, which means friendship. Synonyms: hostility, animosity, antagonism.

gre.s: The ____ between the two clans, rooted in a dispute over land generations earlier, was so bitter that members refused even to attend the same weddings.
gre.clue: so bitter that members refused even to attend the same weddings

example: Years of open enmity ended only when the two retired tennis champions, once bitter rivals, agreed to coach the national youth squad together.

en: Short-lived; fading or disappearing soon after it appears
hook: EPHEMERAL: like an Instagram story, gone in a day.
story: Ephemeral. Lamia posted a dance video on a Tuesday. By Wednesday, it had two million views. Strangers recognised her in the market. A TV channel called. She felt famous. By the following Tuesday, nobody remembered it. The internet had moved on to a dancing goat. Internet fame is ephemeral: lasting for a very short time. Mayflies, soap bubbles, and trends are ephemeral. Mountains and real friendships are not. Synonyms: transient, fleeting, evanescent.

gre.s: Unlike the ____ fashions that vanish within a season, the designer's classic coat has remained popular for over fifty years.
gre.clue: vanish within a season

example: Most viral dance trends are ephemeral, filling every phone screen in Dhaka for a week before they are forgotten entirely.

en: Unreasonably high, especially of price
hook: EX-ORBIT-ANT: prices gone OUT OF ORBIT.
story: Exorbitant. The night before Eid, Imran went to buy a bus ticket home to Rangpur. The usual fare was eight hundred taka. The man at the counter demanded three thousand. Rickshaw fares had tripled, and even a cup of tea cost double. 'These prices are exorbitant,' Imran groaned: unreasonably high. Ex means out of, and orbit means track, so an exorbitant price has wandered right out of its normal orbit. Synonyms: excessive, extortionate, outrageous.

gre.s: Many families who once used the private clinic now avoid it, since its ____ fees put even routine checkups beyond the reach of ordinary workers.
gre.clue: put even routine checkups beyond the reach of ordinary workers

example: The landlord demanded an exorbitant deposit of six months' rent, so the young couple kept searching for another flat in Mirpur.

en: To flatter or please someone excessively to gain favor
hook: FAWN: like a puppy wagging its tail, licking boots.
story: Fawn. Whenever the company chairman visited the branch office, Imran's manager became a different person. He held doors open, laughed loudly at every joke, praised the chairman's tie, and kept saying, 'Excellent idea, sir.' The moment the chairman left, he went back to shouting at everyone. He fawned over the chairman: he flattered him excessively to win favour. Picture an eager puppy wagging its tail. A fawn is also a baby deer, but the verb is about flattery. Synonyms: grovel, toady, kowtow.

gre.s: Whenever the visiting director appeared, the junior staff would ____, laughing politely at his weakest jokes and praising his every remark, while the senior engineers remained coolly professional.
gre.clue: praising his every remark

example: Reporters who fawned over the billionaire at his product launch later struggled to ask him any hard questions about his company's debts.

en: Done openly and shamelessly, so the wrong is impossible to miss
hook: FLAGRANT: as obvious as a FLAG waving in your face.
story: Flagrant. During a televised cricket match, a fielder scratched the ball with a bottle cap right in front of the camera. Millions of viewers saw it clearly in slow motion. There was no doubt and no excuse; it was a flagrant violation of the rules: shockingly obvious and offensive. Flagrant comes from the Latin for burning, like a fire blazing so brightly that nobody can miss it. Do not confuse it with fragrant, which simply smells nice. Synonyms: blatant, glaring, egregious.

gre.s: Far from being a subtle oversight, the company's dumping of chemicals into the river was a ____ violation of environmental law, carried out openly in daylight for years.
gre.clue: carried out openly in daylight for years

example: The referee sent off the defender for a flagrant foul, a reckless late tackle that left the striker lying on the grass.

en: To do without something pleasant; to give up
hook: FOR-GO: let it GO.
story: Forgo. During Ramadan, Imran's office canteen is full of samosas and tea, but he forgoes them all from dawn until sunset. That same year he also forwent a well-paid job offer in Singapore to stay near his ageing parents. To forgo is to do without something pleasant, or to give it up voluntarily. Do not confuse it with forego, which can mean to go before; a foregone conclusion was decided in advance. Synonyms: relinquish, renounce, waive.

gre.s: Determined to finish her dissertation by spring, the doctoral student chose to ____ the holiday trip her friends had planned, staying behind in the library instead.
gre.clue: staying behind in the library instead

example: To pay her younger brother's school fees, Shirin decided to forgo new clothes for Eid two years in a row.

en: To make or do something on the spot without planning ahead
hook: IMPROVISE: IM-PRO-VISE, not foreseen (pro-vise), done on the spot.
story: Improvise. Halfway through Sara's big presentation, the projector died. Two hundred people stared at a blank screen. Sara paused, smiled, picked up a marker, and drew her charts on the whiteboard from memory, telling the story of her research as she went. The audience loved it even more. She had improvised: created or performed something without preparation. Jazz musicians improvise solos. Improvise means unforeseen, done on the spot.

gre.s: When the main speaker failed to arrive, the host was forced to ____, delivering a twenty-minute talk with no notes at all.
gre.clue: with no notes at all

example: When the tent pole snapped during the camping trip, Farhan improvised a replacement from a bamboo stick and some rope.

en: Done carelessly, without choosing or judging with care
hook: IN-DISCRIMINATE: doesn't DISCRIMINATE, doesn't choose carefully.
story: Indiscriminate. Worried about pests, a farmer sprayed pesticide over his entire field, the pond, the trees, and the nearby hedges. He killed the pests. He also killed the bees, the frogs, the birds, and every fish in the pond. His spraying had been indiscriminate: done at random, without careful judgment or selection. In means not, discriminate means to distinguish carefully. Indiscriminate use of antibiotics creates superbugs that no medicine can kill.

gre.s: Critics condemned the ____ bombing campaign, which struck hospitals and markets as readily as military targets.
gre.clue: struck hospitals and markets as readily as military targets

example: Doctors warn that the indiscriminate use of antibiotics, often bought without a prescription, is breeding bacteria that no drug can kill.

en: Curious; eager for knowledge
hook: INQUISITIVE: always INQUIRING.
story: Inquisitive. Mitu's little nephew asked forty questions in a single afternoon. Why is the sky blue? Where do clouds go at night? Why do fish not drown? How does the phone know my voice? He opened every drawer and took apart a broken radio to see what was inside. He was inquisitive: curious and eager for knowledge. Inquisitive shares a root with inquiry and question. It can also suggest being nosy about other people's affairs. Synonyms: curious, inquiring, probing.

gre.s: Endlessly ____, the young scientist pestered her mentors with questions and spent her weekends dismantling old instruments to learn how they worked.
gre.clue: pestered her mentors with questions

example: An inquisitive reader, my grandfather filled the margins of his books with questions he planned to look up later.

en: Deserving praise or reward
hook: MERITORIOUS: full of MERIT.
story: Meritorious. During a flood, a young police constable in Sirajganj waded through chest-deep water for two days, carrying old people and children to safety. He rescued more than sixty villagers. Later he received a medal for meritorious service: deserving praise or reward. Meritorious comes from merit, the quality of deserving. Top students win merit scholarships. Meritorious means more than merely good; it means good enough to earn recognition. Synonyms: praiseworthy, commendable, laudable. Opposite: blameworthy.

gre.s: The committee rejected his nomination, arguing that his work, while competent, was not especially ____ and did nothing to distinguish him from his peers.
gre.clue: did nothing to distinguish him from his peers

example: The fire officer received a medal for meritorious service after pulling six workers from the burning garment factory in Ashulia.

en: Someone overly absorbed in admiring themselves and their looks
hook: NARCISSUS: fell in love with his own reflection.
story: Narcissist. At every family gathering, cousin Sabbir steers the conversation back to himself: his new car, his gym routine, his latest promotion. He checks his reflection in every window and posts ten selfies a day. When someone else shares good news, he looks bored. He is a narcissist: a person excessively interested in himself and his own appearance. In Greek myth, the youth Narcissus fell in love with his own reflection in a pool. Synonyms: egotist, egoist.

gre.s: A thoroughgoing ____, the actor treated every interview as an occasion for self-praise and could rarely sit through a conversation that was not about himself.
gre.clue: could rarely sit through a conversation that was not about himself

example: Only a narcissist would turn a friend's wedding toast into ten minutes about his own career, the guests muttered afterward.

en: Calm and peaceful; not easily upset
hook: PLACID: a PLACE that's calm, like a still lake.
story: Placid. At dawn, the lake at Ramsagar was perfectly placid: not a ripple, just a smooth silver mirror reflecting the trees. Sara's grandmother had the same nature. When the pressure cooker exploded, the children screamed, and the guests arrived early all at once, she simply smiled and said, "Let's have tea." Nothing could disturb her calm. Placid means peaceful and not easily upset. A placid place, a placid temper, a placid face.

gre.s: Despite the chaos surrounding him, the pilot remained ____, calmly guiding the damaged plane to a safe landing.
gre.clue: calmly guiding the damaged plane

example: Even when the toddlers screamed and threw rice across the table, their placid grandmother simply carried on with her story.

en: An expression of extreme enthusiasm; a free-form piece of music
hook: RHAPSODY: Bohemian RHAPSODY — wild, joyful music.
story: Rhapsody. When Joya returned from her first trip to the Sundarbans, she could not stop talking. The mangroves at dawn, the spotted deer, the tiger paw prints in the mud, the stars over the river: she went on for an hour, eyes shining. Her friends teased her for the rhapsody: an expression of extreme enthusiasm. In music, a rhapsody is a free flowing, emotional piece, like Rhapsody in Blue. To rhapsodize is to praise ecstatically. Synonyms: rapture, effusion, ecstasy.

gre.s: The critic, usually so restrained, launched into a ____ about the young violinist, praising her tone and phrasing in such ecstatic terms that readers were astonished.
gre.clue: in such ecstatic terms

example: Her travel blog dissolved into a rhapsody about the tea gardens of Srimangal, with three paragraphs devoted to the morning mist alone.

en: A split or division between groups, often over beliefs
hook: SCHISM (pronounced SIZ-um): a SCISSOR-cut through a group.
story: Schism. For decades, the village cricket club was united. Then a quarrel broke out over whether to accept sponsorship from a tobacco company. Half the members walked out and formed a rival club across the field, and some families stopped speaking to each other. The club suffered a schism: a split or division between groups, often over beliefs. The word is famous for religious splits, like the Great Schism between Eastern and Western Christianity. Synonyms: rift, rupture, breach. Opposite: union.

gre.s: What began as a minor disagreement over doctrine eventually produced a lasting ____ within the movement, as its followers divided into two hostile camps.
gre.clue: as its followers divided into two hostile camps

example: A schism in the chess club over whether to allow speed games led half its members to start a rival group across town.

en: Morally ignoble or dishonorable; dirty and squalid
hook: SORDID: SORE and DIRTY.
story: Sordid. A newspaper investigation revealed a sordid story. A charity that claimed to feed orphans had spent its donations on luxury cars and secret apartments, while the children lived in a damp, rat infested building. Readers were disgusted. Sordid means morally ignoble or dishonorable; it can also mean dirty and squalid, like that orphanage. It comes from the Latin sordes, meaning filth. Synonyms: sleazy, squalid, base, unsavory.

gre.s: The memoir, which promised an inspiring tale of artistic triumph, instead revealed a ____ history of bribery, betrayal, and blackmail.
gre.clue: bribery, betrayal, and blackmail

example: Journalists spent months tracing the sordid deals through which public land in Dhaka was quietly sold to friends of officials.

en: More than needed; unnecessary
hook: SUPER-FLUOUS: flows (flu) OVER (super) the top.
story: Superfluous. Arif's first draft described the building as "very extremely big huge enormous." His editor deleted four words and left one: "enormous." The rest were superfluous: more than needed, unnecessary. Super means over, fluous means flowing: flowing over the top of the cup. A superfluous remark adds nothing to a conversation. Good GRE essays contain no superfluous words.

gre.s: The editor cut several paragraphs that she considered ____, since they merely repeated points made earlier in the chapter.
gre.clue: merely repeated points made earlier

example: Apologizing again would be superfluous, Mitu decided, since her sister had already forgiven her the night before.

en: Very weak or slight
hook: TENUOUS: as THIN as a thread.
story: Tenuous. Tania, a young lawyer, studied the case against her client. The only evidence was that someone saw a man in a blue shirt near the shop that night, and half of Dhaka owns a blue shirt. The link between her client and the theft was tenuous: very weak or slight. Tenuous comes from the Latin tenuis, meaning thin, like a thin thread that could snap at any moment. A tenuous grip, a tenuous argument. Synonyms: flimsy, slender, shaky.

gre.s: The prosecutor's case rested on a ____ chain of circumstantial evidence, and the defense easily broke it by showing that the key witness had been miles away.
gre.clue: the defense easily broke it

example: The village's tenuous internet connection dropped every few minutes, making Rakib's online exam a test of patience as much as knowledge.

en: Real; used to emphasize that a description is accurate
hook: VERITABLE: VERY TRUE (veritas = truth).
story: Veritable. Sara opened her grandfather's old trunk expecting dusty clothes. Instead she found letters from 1971, black and white photographs of freedom fighters, a hand-drawn map of their village, and a diary covering forty years. It was a veritable treasure trove of family history. Veritable emphasizes that a description, even a dramatic one, is truly accurate. Think of verity, meaning truth, as in verify. A veritable feast, a veritable genius. Synonyms: real, genuine, true.

gre.s: The once-neglected archive has become a ____ goldmine for historians: scholars have already uncovered hundreds of documents previously thought lost.
gre.clue: scholars have already uncovered hundreds of documents previously thought lost

example: Grandma's kitchen became a veritable factory before Eid, turning out hundreds of pitha for relatives, neighbors, and the night guards.

en: Showing great energy and enthusiasm for a cause or goal
hook: ZEALOUS: full of ZEAL (passion).
story: Zealous. The blood donation camp needed volunteers, and Zayan signed up. He arrived first every morning and left last every night. He carried the heaviest boxes, made posters, and personally convinced fifty friends to donate. When supplies ran low, he cycled across the city to fetch more. Zealous means full of energetic enthusiasm for a cause or goal. Zeal means passion. A zealot is someone whose zeal becomes extreme and fanatical.

gre.s: The new inspector was so ____ in enforcing the regulations that he fined shops for violations his predecessors had ignored for years.
gre.clue: fined shops for violations his predecessors had ignored for years

example: A zealous volunteer, Imran spent every weekend of the dengue season knocking on doors to warn families about standing water.
